title: Anxiety before a storm, trip, or hunt
def: Worry before a storm or a big trip is common; preparing, planning, and calming the body bring it down to a useful level.
look: checking the forecast over and over
use: Make a short checklist, do one preparation step, then do something calming such as slow breathing or a walk.
not: Do not let worry push you into skipping sleep or food before a trip.
call: Talk to a clinician if anxiety gets in the way of daily life. Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Slow breathing and grounding
def: Slow breathing and grounding are simple ways to calm a racing body and mind: breathe out longer than in, and notice what is around you.
look: breathing in for about four counts, out for six
naming five things you see, four you hear, three you can touch
shoulders dropping as the body settles
use: Sit or stand steady, breathe slowly for a few minutes, and name what you sense around you.
not: This does not replace medical care for chest pain or trouble breathing.

title: Low mood in short winter days or isolation
def: Many people feel lower in short, dark days or in isolation; some have seasonal affective disorder, a form of depression that returns each winter.
look: low energy, oversleeping, and craving carbohydrates in winter
loss of interest that lasts weeks
use: Get outside in daylight, move your body, keep regular sleep and meals, and stay in touch with people.
not: Do not ignore weeks of low mood or thoughts of self-harm.
call: See a clinician if low mood lasts two weeks or more. Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Loneliness
def: Loneliness is the painful feeling of being disconnected; it is common and it affects health, and small regular contact helps.
look: long stretches without talking to anyone
use: Reach out to one person today, join a regular activity, help someone else, and keep in touch on a schedule.
not: Do not wait for others to reach out first.
call: 988 is also there if you just need to talk. Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Anger and conflict in a family or group under stress
def: Stress, hunger, cold, and fatigue shorten tempers; groups do better when they pause, meet basic needs, and decide calmly.
use: Take a break, eat and warm up, let each person speak, and agree on one next step together.
not: Do not make safety decisions in the middle of a fight, and keep firearms unloaded when tempers rise.
call: Call 911 if anyone is threatened or hurt.

title: Shame after a mistake
def: After a mistake, shame can feel overwhelming; owning what happened, making it right where you can, and learning from it is healthier than self-punishment.
use: Name what happened, take one step to repair or learn, and talk to someone you trust.
not: Do not punish yourself with risky behavior or isolation.
call: Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Caregiver or parent burnout in a long outage
def: Caring for others through a long outage or crisis drains people; burnout shows up as exhaustion, irritability, and feeling numb.
look: no time to eat or sleep yourself
snapping at people you care for
use: Share tasks, take short breaks, eat and sleep when you can, and ask neighbors or relatives for help.
not: Do not skip your own medicines, food, or rest.
call: Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Finding help for lasting trauma
def: When nightmares, flashbacks, or avoidance last more than a month after a frightening event, it may be post-traumatic stress, and effective treatment exists.
look: feeling on edge most of the time
use: Talk to a doctor or a licensed mental health professional; veterans can use VA services, and SAMHSA's helpline can point to local care.
not: Do not try to manage it alone with alcohol or drugs.
call: SAMHSA's National Helpline, 1-800-662-4357. Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Routines that keep morale up
def: Simple routines such as regular meals, daylight, movement, shared tasks, and time with others keep morale steady through long hard periods.
look: a daily walk or chore outside
a moment to talk or laugh together
use: Set a daily rhythm, give everyone a job, and mark small successes.
not: Do not let days blur into no structure for weeks.

title: Support for veterans
def: Veterans and their families can reach the Veterans Crisis Line by calling 988 and pressing 1, by text, or by chat, and VA offers mental health care.
look: a veteran withdrawing or drinking more
use: Call 988 and press 1, or text 838255, and connect with VA mental health services.
not: Do not wait for a crisis to reach out.
call: Veterans Crisis Line: dial 988 then press 1, or text 838255. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Stress after a disaster
def: After a disaster, people often feel anxious, sad, angry, or numb, have trouble sleeping, and worry about money and home; support and time help most recover.
look: feeling overwhelmed by cleanup and paperwork
use: Take care of basics, stay connected, limit news, take breaks from cleanup, and use crisis counseling if you need it.
not: Do not ignore lasting distress or thoughts of self-harm.
call: SAMHSA's Disaster Distress Helpline: call or text 1-800-985-5990. Call or text 988 any time for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; veterans can press 1. Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
